H1B is a weird status, called 'dual intent'. You are here temporarily but can seek permanent resident status nonetheless.

Employers bringing in H1B thus have both a carrot and a stick:

The stick is that should you lose your job, you lose your legal status and have 15 days to leave the country. Now you can jump ship, and transfer to another employer willing to sponsor you, but that's a high risk move.

The carrot is that said employer promises to sponsor you for permanent resident status (green card); now, a H1B is valid 3 years, and may be renewed once (you can have some extra time at the end if you are far enough along in the gc application process, but not much...); in that sense, it's an improvement over indentured servitude which were seven years deals. :-)

It so happens that the application process for the gc takes - guess what - about six years. It might go faster - and there are faster tracks to gc depending on your background - but it is not in the interest of the employer to speed things up anyway. Why is that important? well, if you transfer to another employer, you have to restart the whole gc application from scratch, but the clock keeps ticking on the 3+3 years H1B expiration date. Which makes seeking employment elsewhere a high risk move, one you can only do early on in the process (unless you don't care about leaving at the end that is). A very scary stick indeed.

All this makes for very compliant employees, very unlikely to rock the boat.

ps so it is intended for high skilled workers (and super models :-) ) - but is indeed used to bring in people at lower than market value wages. Sure, there are rules about having to pay them market value, but these rules are extremely easily circumvented; especially in high tech.
